title: Why · How · What
caption: Why AI needs a brief, how five moves and five principles give it one, and what the Explorable shows.

why.title: You brief an AI, and it forgets, guesses and still sounds sure.
why.caption: <marker>Every new chat starts from zero, and when it is unsure it answers anyway instead of asking.</marker> Five traits, PRICE, explain why it costs you, side by side for a freelancer and for AI.

how.title: Five moves brief one agent: BRIEF.
how.caption: <marker>Break it down, put requirements first, interview yourself with AI, evaluate each step and start fresh for each piece.</marker> Each move counters one or more of the five traits.

what.title: Five principles run the work across stages: BRACE.
what.caption: <marker>Start backwards from the goal, resolve dependencies early, give autonomy through intent, agree contracts at the seams and engineer trust.</marker> See them on DRIVE: Define, Reason, Implement, Verify, Evolve.

why.header: The forgetting and the guessing are built in
why.description: The context window is the model's working memory, and memory across chats exists only where an application stores notes and puts them back, because the memory tool runs client-side [1][2]. Most benchmarks score a guess above an abstention, so training rewards guessing instead of asking [3] (Episode evidence: Pay the price).

kalai-why-models-hallucinate.title: Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate

how.header: Each move has evidence behind it
how.description: Solving simpler subproblems in sequence scored 99% or better on a compositional benchmark against 16% for chain-of-thought prompting with an older model [1]. Results varied more than twice as much for a requirement left unstated as for one stated [2]. Feedback on each reasoning step beats feedback on the final result alone [3]. Top models scored on average 39% lower in multi-turn conversation than with the full instruction at once [4] (Episode evidence: Manage the price). "Interview yourself with AI" is backed by two further studies there.

what.header: BRACE: five principles, each with its own source
what.description: Anthropic tells builders to define success criteria up front [1]. Planning backwards from the goal is established practice in planning, but no study tests it on agent work (research PLAN-0003). Subagents without detailed tasks "duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information", and multi-agent systems are a poor fit where many dependencies run between agents [2] (research SWE-0007, SWE-0008). Army doctrine tells commanders to state the results to be attained, not how, and says trust "must be earned" [3] (research AIE-0027). Reliance should match demonstrated reliability [4], and agents need checkpoints, guardrails and ground truth from the environment [5] (research AIE-0028).
